title: Hobbes: The State of Nature and the Leviathan
subtitle: Why frightened, equal, self-interested people would agree to create a giant
objectives: By the end you will be able to describe Hobbes's life and the civil war that shaped his thinking.
Explain his materialism: the view that everything, including human thought, is matter in motion.
Reconstruct his argument that life in a state of nature would be a war of all against all, “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.”
Explain the social contract that creates the sovereign, and why Hobbes thought that sovereign must be so powerful.
Evaluate the main objections to Hobbes, from Locke's lions to modern evidence about cooperation.
hook:
Here is a thought experiment. Tomorrow morning, every government on Earth vanishes. No police, no courts, no army, no laws, no one to enforce a contract or punish a theft. Nothing else changes: people are just as they are now, with the same needs, fears and ambitions. What happens next?

Maybe you picture neighbors cooperating, sharing food, organizing themselves peacefully. Or maybe you picture locked doors, hoarding, gangs, and a lot of people buying weapons. Thomas Hobbes, writing in the 1640s while his country was tearing itself apart in civil war, was sure he knew the answer. And from that answer he built one of the most powerful arguments in the history of political philosophy: an argument for why we should obey the state at all.

sections.heading: Born Twin to Fear
sections.body:
**Thomas Hobbes** was born on 5 April 1588 in Westport, next to Malmesbury in Wiltshire, England. That spring all England was waiting in dread for the Spanish Armada, the vast invasion fleet sent by Philip II of Spain. In a Latin verse autobiography written in old age, Hobbes said that his mother was so frightened by the rumors that she gave birth to twins: himself and fear. It is a joke, but a revealing one. Fear is at the center of his philosophy.

He studied at Oxford, which he found dull and full of Aristotle, and then spent most of his long life as a tutor and secretary to the aristocratic Cavendish family, the Earls of Devonshire. The job gave him books, leisure and travel. On tours of Europe he met leading thinkers; in 1636 he visited Galileo in Florence (Day 41), and he joined the intellectual circle of Marin Mersenne in Paris, where he later wrote one of the sets of objections to Descartes' *Meditations* (Day 43).

A famous story, told by his friend the biographer John Aubrey, says that at about forty Hobbes happened to see a copy of Euclid's *Elements* open in a gentleman's library at a proposition he thought impossible. He traced the proof back step by step until he was convinced, and fell in love with geometry. Whether or not every detail is true, geometry became his model: start with clear definitions and build conclusions that no one can reasonably deny.

Then politics exploded. Tensions between King Charles I and Parliament were mounting, and Hobbes, known as a defender of royal power, fled to Paris in 1640, later claiming he was the first of all that fled. Civil war broke out in 1642. In 1649 the king was put on trial and beheaded. In Paris, Hobbes briefly tutored the exiled Prince of Wales, the future Charles II, in mathematics. In 1651 he published his masterpiece, *Leviathan*, and soon returned to England, now ruled by Parliament and Oliver Cromwell.

Hobbes lived to ninety-one, writing on geometry, physics and history, quarreling with mathematicians, and translating Homer in his eighties. He was widely accused of atheism, and after the Great Fire of London in 1666 a parliamentary committee even considered his writings. He died in 1679.

sections.heading: Everything Is Matter in Motion
sections.body:
Hobbes built his politics on a complete philosophy of nature. He was a thoroughgoing **materialist**: he held that everything that exists is a body, matter in motion. There are no immaterial souls, no Aristotelian forms or purposes, no disembodied spirits. (He was careful to say that God, too, was a kind of body, a position that convinced few people of his piety.)

The opening of *Leviathan* sets out the picture. Nature, he says, is the art by which God made and governs the world, and human beings imitate it. We make automata, engines that move themselves by springs and wheels like a watch. Why not say they have an artificial life? For what is the heart, he asks, but a spring, the nerves but so many strings, and the joints but so many wheels? Life is just a motion of limbs.

This is the mechanical worldview of the Scientific Revolution (Day 41) applied to human beings. Perception, for Hobbes, is the effect of motions from outside bodies pressing on our sense organs. Imagination is decaying sense, the fading of those motions, like ripples dying away after the wind drops. Thinking is a kind of calculation; reasoning, he wrote, is nothing but reckoning, adding and subtracting names. (Some have seen in this an ancestor of the idea of computer thinking.)

And emotions? They are motions too: small beginnings of movement toward things, which we call desire or appetite, or away from things, which we call aversion. What we call good is simply whatever we desire; evil is whatever we are averse to. There is no good in itself written into the universe, no Form of the Good (Day 11) and no natural purpose of human life (Day 20).

This makes Hobbes's ethics strikingly different from Plato's and Aristotle's. For them, politics aimed at the good life, at virtue and flourishing. For Hobbes, human beings have no shared highest good. What they do share is a supreme evil to avoid: violent death. Politics must be built not on a vision of the good but on that common fear.

sections.heading: The State of Nature: The War of All Against All
sections.body:
In chapter 13 of *Leviathan* Hobbes asks the question of our hook. Imagine human beings without any common power over them, a condition he calls the **state of nature**. What would it be like?

He starts with a surprising premise: people are roughly **equal**. Not in the sense that everyone is equally strong or clever, but equal enough that the weakest can kill the strongest, either by a secret plot or by teaming up with others. No one is safe because no one is strong enough to be invulnerable.

From equality of ability comes equality of hope. If two people want the same thing, and both cannot have it, they become enemies. Hobbes names three principal causes of quarrel in human nature:

1. **Competition**, which makes people attack for gain.
2. **Diffidence**, meaning distrust or insecurity, which makes people attack for safety. If you suspect your neighbor might attack you, the rational move may be to strike first.
3. **Glory**, which makes people attack for reputation, over trifles like a word, a smile or a sign of disrespect.

The second cause is the most chilling. Even if most people are peaceful, the mere possibility that some are not forces everyone to be on guard, and the best defense may be offense. The result is a condition of war of every man against every man. War, Hobbes adds, does not consist only in actual fighting, just as bad weather is not a single shower; it is a known disposition to fight, with no assurance to the contrary.

Then comes the most famous passage in English political philosophy. In such a condition, Hobbes writes, there is no place for industry, because its fruit is uncertain; no agriculture, no navigation, no building, no knowledge, no arts, no letters, no society, and, worst of all, continual fear and danger of violent death, and the life of man, **solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short**.

In the state of nature, Hobbes adds, nothing can be unjust. Where there is no common power, there is no law, and where there is no law, there is no injustice. Everyone has a **right of nature**, a liberty to use their own power to preserve themselves, even a right to everything, including one another's bodies.

sections.heading: Do You Really Believe This? Hobbes's Evidence
sections.body:
Hobbes knew readers would find this picture insulting. So he asked them to check it against their own behavior. When you set out on a journey, he says, you arm yourself and try to travel in company; when you go to sleep, you lock your doors; even in your own house, you lock your chests. And you do this knowing there are laws and armed officers to punish any wrong done to you. What opinion of your fellow citizens does that show? Do you not accuse mankind by your actions as much as I do by my words?

He also pointed to evidence of three kinds:

- **Civil war**, which his own generation was living through, showing what happens when a common power collapses.
- **Relations between kings and states**, which have no common power above them and so stand in a posture of gladiators, weapons pointed and eyes fixed on one another, with forts, garrisons and spies on their frontiers. This is the origin of what international relations scholars call the realist view of world politics.
- **Indigenous peoples of America**, whom he wrongly described as living without government. This claim was ignorant and prejudiced: many Native American societies had complex political institutions. Modern readers rightly reject it.

Hobbes did not claim that the whole human race had once lived in a single state of nature at some historical moment. The state of nature is mainly a **thought experiment**, a way of seeing what government is for by imagining its absence. The question is not what happened long ago but what would happen if the state dissolved tomorrow.

Notice also what Hobbes is *not* saying. He does not claim that people are wicked by nature; he explicitly denies that the desires and passions are sins in themselves. His argument works even if most people are decent. The problem is structural: in a world without enforcement, even good people must act defensively, and defensive action looks like aggression to others. Modern game theorists call this kind of trap a **security dilemma** or a prisoner's dilemma, situations where each person's rational choice leaves everyone worse off.

sections.heading: The Social Contract and the Mortal God
sections.body:
How do we escape? Hobbes says that reason suggests convenient articles of peace, which he calls **laws of nature**: general rules, discovered by reason, telling us what we must do to preserve our lives. The first is to seek peace when you can, and use the advantages of war when you cannot. The second is to be willing, when others are too, to lay down your right to all things, and be content with as much liberty against others as you would allow them against you. The third is that people perform the covenants they make; this, Hobbes says, is the origin of justice.

But here is the catch. In the state of nature, why would anyone keep a promise? If I disarm first and you don't, I am dead. In one of his most quoted lines (chapter 17), Hobbes says that covenants without the sword are but words, and of no strength to secure a man at all.

The solution is a **social contract**: an agreement in which each person, in effect, says to every other: I authorize this man, or this assembly, and give up my right of governing myself to him, on condition that you do the same. The multitude so united becomes a single person, a commonwealth, which Hobbes calls the great **Leviathan**, after the sea monster of the Book of Job, or rather, he says with reverence, that **mortal god** to which we owe our peace and defense under the immortal God.

The famous title page of *Leviathan* shows a crowned giant towering over a landscape, holding a sword and a bishop's crozier; look closely and his body is made of hundreds of tiny people. The state is us, unified into one artificial person.

The one who bears this authority is the **sovereign**. Because the subjects have authorized all the sovereign's actions, the sovereign cannot, strictly speaking, wrong them; they would be complaining of their own acts. The sovereign controls law, property, war and peace, the censorship of dangerous doctrines, and even the public teaching of religion. Hobbes preferred monarchy, but his argument works for any undivided sovereign, including an assembly. What he could not accept was divided sovereignty, king against Parliament, church against state, which he believed had caused the civil war. A kingdom divided against itself, he warned, cannot stand.

sections.heading: Limits, Objections and Legacy
sections.body:
Is Hobbes simply a defender of tyranny? Not quite. The whole point of the contract is self-preservation, so some rights cannot be given away. A subject may resist those who come to kill, wound or imprison him, and is not bound to accuse himself. And if the sovereign can no longer protect its subjects, their obligation ends, since protection is the reason for obedience. This last point was controversial: it allowed Hobbes to accept Cromwell's government once the king's cause was lost, and royalists accused him of disloyalty.

Still, the objections are serious.

- **The lions objection.** John Locke (Day 52) replied, in effect, that it is strange to think people would take care to protect themselves from polecats and foxes, the petty harms of their neighbors, but be content, even think it safety, to be devoured by lions, an all-powerful ruler. Absolute power may be more dangerous than anarchy.
- **Too dark a picture of human nature.** Rousseau (Day 53) accused Hobbes of projecting the vices of competitive civilized people back onto natural humanity. Anthropology and evolutionary psychology show that humans are also deeply cooperative, empathetic and norm-following.
- **Cooperation without a Leviathan.** The political economist Elinor Ostrom, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2009, studied communities around the world that successfully managed shared resources like fisheries and pastures for centuries without a central sovereign, using local rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions.
- **A problem of logic.** If people in the state of nature cannot trust each other to keep promises, how can they trust each other enough to make the founding contract?

Yet Hobbes's achievement is enormous. He was the first major thinker to build political authority entirely from the consent of free and equal individuals rather than from divine right, tradition or nature's hierarchy. Remember Glaucon's story in Plato's *Republic* (Day 13), that justice is a compromise people make to avoid suffering injustice? Hobbes turned that suggestion into a full theory. The **social contract** tradition he founded runs through Locke (Day 52), Rousseau (Day 53) and Kant to John Rawls (Day 82). And his blunt question, why should anyone obey the state, remains the first question of political philosophy.

keyQuote.text: And the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.

modernConnection.title: Failed States, Online Platforms and the Pull of the Leviathan
modernConnection.body:
We do not have to imagine the state of nature entirely. When states collapse, Hobbes's prediction often comes uncomfortably close to reality. In Somalia after 1991, in parts of Syria and Libya after their civil wars, and in the gang-controlled neighborhoods of some cities, the disappearance of an effective common power has typically brought armed factions, insecurity, hoarding and the flight of investment, just as Hobbes said: no place for industry, because its fruit is uncertain. Political scientists who study **failed states** often describe a scramble for protection, and people frequently welcome even a harsh authority if it restores order, as Hobbes predicted.

International politics is a second laboratory. There is no world government, and the **realist** school of international relations, from Hans Morgenthau to John Mearsheimer, explicitly draws on Hobbes to explain why states arm themselves and distrust one another even when none wants war. The nuclear standoff of the Cold War was a vast security dilemma.

A third, smaller laboratory is online. Early internet idealists imagined that cyberspace would govern itself. Instead, unmoderated spaces often fill up with spam, harassment and scams, and platforms have become private sovereigns, writing the rules, enforcing them and banishing offenders, usually with little accountability. Debates about content moderation are, in part, debates about how much Leviathan we need and who should control it.

But the analogy has limits, and they matter. In real failed states, the violence is usually organized by groups, often armed by outside powers, not a war of isolated individuals. And plenty of communities, from Ostrom's fishing villages to Wikipedia's volunteer editors, achieve order through shared norms, reputation and decentralized enforcement. Even the steep historical decline in violent death that Steven Pinker described in *The Better Angels of Our Nature* (2011), which he partly credits to strong states, is debated by historians and anthropologists. The modern lesson may be that Hobbes was right that order needs enforcement, but wrong that it must come from a single absolute sovereign.

vocabulary.definition: The view that everything that exists is matter (for Hobbes, bodies in motion), with no immaterial souls or spirits.
vocabulary.example: Hobbes's materialism led him to describe thinking as a kind of reckoning carried out by the body.

vocabulary.definition: The condition of human beings without any common political authority over them; for Hobbes, mainly a thought experiment showing why government is needed.
vocabulary.example: Hobbes argued that the state of nature would be a war of all against all.

vocabulary.definition: In Hobbes's usage, distrust or insecurity about others, which leads people to strike first for their own safety.
vocabulary.example: Diffidence explains why even peaceful people might arm themselves when no one can guarantee their safety.

vocabulary.definition: For Hobbes, each person's liberty to use their own power to preserve their life, which in the state of nature extends to a right to everything.
vocabulary.example: In the state of nature, the right of nature means no one can be accused of injustice for defending themselves.

vocabulary.definition: For Hobbes, a general rule discovered by reason telling people what they must do to preserve their lives, such as seeking peace and keeping covenants.
vocabulary.example: The first law of nature tells us to seek peace whenever there is hope of obtaining it.

vocabulary.definition: An agreement, real or hypothetical, by which individuals create political authority and accept obligations to obey it.
vocabulary.example: Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau all used the idea of a social contract to explain why government is legitimate.

vocabulary.definition: The person or assembly holding supreme, undivided political authority, created by the social contract to keep the peace.
vocabulary.example: For Hobbes, the sovereign must control the army, the courts and even public teaching.

vocabulary.definition: A situation in which actions one party takes to make itself safer make others feel less safe, leading to escalating mutual threat.
vocabulary.example: Two neighboring states building up their armies for defense can trap themselves in a security dilemma.

thinkingExercise.title: The Island Without Rules
thinkingExercise.prompt: Imagine that two hundred strangers from many countries are stranded on a large island with enough resources to survive, but no rescue in sight and no existing authority. Using Hobbes's ideas, think through what would happen and what kind of government, if any, you would argue for.
steps: List what you think would happen in the first month. Where do Hobbes's three causes of quarrel (competition, diffidence, glory) show up, and where might cooperation arise instead?
Write down three rules you would propose to the group. Which of them match Hobbes's laws of nature?
Decide who or what should enforce the rules: one leader, an elected council, everyone together, or no one. Give Hobbes's argument for your choice and Locke's lions objection against it.
Name one right you would refuse to give up to whoever governs the island, and explain why. Then reflect: is your answer closer to Hobbes or to his critics?

summary: Hobbes (1588–1679) wrote Leviathan (1651) in the shadow of the English Civil War, seeking a rational foundation for political order modeled on geometry.
He was a materialist who saw human beings as machines driven by appetite and aversion, with no shared highest good but a shared fear of violent death.
Without a common power, he argued, rough equality, competition, distrust and glory would produce a war of all against all in which life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.
Reason's laws of nature lead people to a social contract that authorizes an absolute, undivided sovereign, because covenants without the sword are but words.

Critics object that absolute power is more dangerous than anarchy, that humans are more cooperative than Hobbes allows, and that communities can create order without a Leviathan; yet Hobbes founded the modern social contract tradition.

quiz.question: Which historical event most directly shaped Hobbes's Leviathan?
options: The English Civil War and the execution of Charles I
quiz.explanation: Hobbes wrote Leviathan in Paris during and after the English Civil War (1642–51), which convinced him that divided authority leads to catastrophe.

quiz.question: What does Hobbes mean by saying people are roughly equal in the state of nature?
options: Everyone has equal moral worth in God's eyes
Even the weakest can kill the strongest, by plotting or allying with others
quiz.explanation: Hobbes's equality is about vulnerability: no one is strong enough to be safe, which is why everyone has reason to fear.

quiz.question: A shopkeeper in a lawless town hires armed guards and attacks a rival gang preemptively, not out of greed but because he fears they will attack him first. Which of Hobbes's causes of quarrel is this?
quiz.explanation: Diffidence (distrust) leads people to attack for safety, striking first because they cannot be sure of others' intentions.

quiz.question: Hobbes argued that human beings are wicked and sinful by nature, which is why the state of nature is so terrible.
quiz.explanation: Hobbes denied that passions are sins in themselves; the problem is structural, since without enforcement even decent people must act defensively.

quiz.question: What did Hobbes mean when he wrote that covenants without the sword are but words?
options: Without a power to enforce them, agreements give no real security
Written contracts matter more than spoken ones
quiz.explanation: In the state of nature, no one can safely keep a promise unless others are compelled to keep theirs, so a common power is needed.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes Hobbes's materialism?
options: Only ideas in the mind are real
Everything that exists, including human thought, is matter in motion
Matter is an illusion created by God
The soul is immortal and separate from the body
quiz.explanation: Hobbes treated perception, imagination, reasoning and emotion as motions of the body, in line with the new mechanical science.

quiz.question: For Hobbes, subjects keep the right to resist someone who comes to kill them, even if that person acts on the sovereign's orders.
quiz.explanation: Since the contract exists for self-preservation, the right to defend one's own life cannot be given away.

quiz.question: John Locke's objection about polecats, foxes and lions is aimed at which part of Hobbes's theory?
options: His claim that people are roughly equal
His demand for an absolute sovereign to protect us from one another
quiz.explanation: Locke argued it is irrational to guard against small dangers from neighbors by submitting to the far greater danger of unlimited power.

quiz.question: Elinor Ostrom's research on fisheries and pastures is often cited against Hobbes because it shows:
options: Communities can sustain cooperation through local rules and monitoring without an absolute sovereign
quiz.explanation: Ostrom documented long-lasting self-governance of shared resources, suggesting order does not always require a single all-powerful ruler.

quiz.question: Hobbes's state of nature is mainly a thought experiment about what life would be like without a common power, rather than a claim about a single historical period.
quiz.explanation: Hobbes used it to show what government is for by imagining its absence, though he also pointed to civil war and international relations as real examples.

goDeeper.body:
Is Hobbes's argument really about self-interest? Twentieth-century scholars sharply disagreed. A. E. Taylor and Howard Warrender argued that Hobbes's laws of nature are genuine moral obligations, ultimately grounded in God's command, so that Hobbes is closer to the natural law tradition of Aquinas (Day 36) than he appears. Most later interpreters, like David Gauthier and Gregory Kavka, read him instead as a rational choice theorist: the laws of nature are simply the rules a prudent, self-interested person would follow. On this reading Hobbes anticipates modern game theory, and the state of nature looks like a many-person prisoner's dilemma.

This leads to the famous problem of the Fool. In chapter 15, Hobbes imagines a Fool who says in his heart that there is no such thing as justice and that breaking a covenant is reasonable whenever it pays. Hobbes replies that the covenant-breaker cannot reasonably expect to be accepted into any society that offers defense, and so gambles his life on others' mistakes. Philosophers still debate whether this reply works, and the question, whether it is ever rational to be moral when you could get away with cheating, is the Ring of Gyges problem from Plato (Day 13) in new clothing.

Another lively debate concerns religion. Half of *Leviathan* is about scripture and the church, and Hobbes argues the sovereign must control public worship. Was he a sincere if unusual Christian, a cautious deist, or an atheist in disguise, as his enemies claimed? The scholar Quentin Skinner has also traced how Hobbes's views on rhetoric shifted, from distrust of eloquence to using it brilliantly in *Leviathan* itself.

readings.title: Leviathan
readings.author: Thomas Hobbes
readings.note: Read the Introduction and chapters 13–17, which contain the state of nature, the laws of nature and the creation of the commonwealth.

readings.title: Hobbes: A Very Short Introduction
readings.author: Richard Tuck
readings.note: A compact, reliable guide to Hobbes's life, science and politics.

readings.title: Governing the Commons
readings.author: Elinor Ostrom
readings.note: The classic study of communities that cooperate without a Leviathan; a powerful empirical challenge to Hobbes.

readings.author: Gregory S. Kavka
readings.note: A rigorous game-theoretic reconstruction of Hobbes's argument, for ambitious readers.

questions: If governments vanished tomorrow, do you think life would be closer to Hobbes's war of all against all or to cooperative self-organization? What evidence would decide the question?
Is it ever rational to obey a ruler you consider unjust? Where would Hobbes draw the line, and where would you?
Big technology platforms act like private sovereigns online. Should their power be limited, and by whom?
